title: Rhinoceros horn is a plane logarithmic spiral from constant front-to-back growth ratio

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Rhinoceros horn is a plane logarithmic spiral from constant front-to-back growth ratio

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The rhinoceros horn grows faster anteriorly than posteriorly in a constant ratio, so it curves as a logarithmic spiral; lying in the median plane, it has no lateral twist and forms a plane spiral.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: v_{ant}/v_{post} = \text{const} \Rightarrow plane spiral r = a e^{\theta\cot\alpha}

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Its longitudinal growth proceeds with a maximum velocity anteriorly, and a minimum posteriorly; and the ratio of these velocities being constant, the horn curves into the form of a logarithmic spiral in the manner that we have already studied.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XIII, “The Shapes of Horns, and of Teeth or Tusks: with a Note on Torsion”; topic “The rhinoceros horn”. Scope: rhinoceros horns

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: v_{ant}/v_{post} = \text{const} \Rightarrow plane spiral r = a e^{\theta\cot\alpha}

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch13-01: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.64

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The shape and growth-ratio predictions are quantitative, but available public data are more likely to resolve geometry than the causal growth field. A targeted compilation could test selected species.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit plane logarithmic and alternative curves to 3D rhinoceros horn centerlines and estimate anterior-posterior increment widths along growth rings. Constant differential-growth ratios coupled to stable spiral parameters would support the claim; lateral torsion, nonlogarithmic fit or changing ratios would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Few digitized horns preserve measurable growth increments.

Museum sampling across ages and species is limited.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A plane logarithmic spiral is a direct fit to a horn outline, and photographs of intact sheaths exist in museum portals. Open 3D coverage of complete rhinoceros horns is thin, and growth velocities at the front and back of the germinal surface are not archived. The geometric half can be checked for the specimens that retain the sheath; the growth-ratio mechanism stays an interpretation of that fit.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit a plane logarithmic spiral to rhinoceros horn sheaths in lateral view and test whether the axis stays in the median plane. A constant angle lying in that plane would support the geometric claim; a helical component, or an angle that changes along the horn, would refute it. The anterior-to-posterior growth ratio is then read from the angle rather than measured as a growth rate.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A constant spiral angle implies a constant growth ratio only inside Thompson's growth model.

Keratin sheaths are often removed from skeletal specimens, so scans capture the core and not the curve Thompson describes.
